Paramour

PAIR-uh-moor · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Paramour is a lover, usually in a secret or improper relationship.

In the novel, the countess risks everything to send one final letter to her paramour before her husband returns from abroad.

Worked Example

In the play, the general secretly visits his paramour every evening after the court has gone to bed, risking his marriage and his title for a few stolen hours.

A paramour is specifically a lover in a relationship that's kept secret or considered improper -- here, one the general is risking everything to keep hidden.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — par-

prefix — par-: by, through (Old French)

root — amour

root — amour: love (Old French, from Latin amor)

Put it together

Put it together: Paramour comes from Old French par amour, literally 'by love' or 'for love's sake' -- it originally just meant 'sweetheart,' but narrowed over the centuries to mean a lover in a secret or forbidden relationship.

Use the root in a new word: amorous

Use the root in a new word: amorous: The amorous teenager left a trail of handwritten notes in his crush's locker every day that week.

Root Check

Word Choice

Paramour carries a slightly old-fashioned, literary flavor and usually implies the relationship is secret or socially disapproved of -- it's rarely used for an openly acknowledged partner.
